story:
He sat inside Capitol Studios in Los Angeles, the light low and warm through the control room windows, a piano nearby and a small cluster of synths humming like a steady breath. Frank had been quiet for a long while, carrying a year of writer’s block like a folded letter in his pocket, and yet here he was, building something else at the same time he was building music. Around him the team moved softly. Christophe Chassol was at the piano, a simple repeated motif taking shape, and the microphones were open for whatever might come through. The memory of that day is not loud; it is the hush before a voice decides to tell its story.

The song grew out of that hush. At first there was the loop, a repeating synth line that had been aired earlier during the livestream when Frank labored on the spiral staircase for the Endless visual. The music was spare, piano and synth and space, and in that space Frank began to speak rather than sing. He let language pour along like someone tracing the edges of a memory, a stream-of-consciousness rap that moved through names and images. He named Apple Jacks, clothing, Palestine, The Geto Boys, The Neptunes, each line like a small stone thrown into a quiet pool. Production came slowly around it. Stwo, Frank Dukes, and Ging added textures that felt patient and unobtrusive, letting Christophe Chassol’s piano remain a warm center while the repeating synth carried the songs steady pulse. The sessions at Capitol were meticulous but relaxed, the kind of work where nothing was forced and everything was earned.

There were challenges, because making a song this honest is like carving a window into your own life. Frank had been pushed through a creative fog for a year, and a childhood friend’s simple urging to consider his upbringing opened a door. Writing became not an attempt to impress, but a way to remember. The visual component was built at the same time, a spiral staircase becoming a living backdrop as the recording unfolded, so the music and the image learned to breathe together. Discovery arrived in small moments: a line that landed true, the way a synth loop echoed a thought, the dry clarity when a verse shifted from memory to present observation. There was no chorus to lean on, no tidy refrain; instead three verses carried the listener like three steps up that staircase, each step steady and revealing.

At the heart of the song there is a gentle insisting on identity and on the fragments that make a person who they are. Frank does not explain everything. He offers scenes and impressions the way a friend offers a photograph. The title nods to Queen Latifah’s song in name alone, but this is a different kind of address. It is intimate and sometimes playful, sometimes sharp, always candid. The song feels autobiographical not because it lists dates or events, but because it places the listener inside small, honest details. That is where its warmth lives: in the recognition that personal memory can be both ordinary and strange, a childhood cereal and a political reference sitting side by side, and that both belong to the same life.

When the visual album Endless was released on June 16, 2016, this track arrived not as a single but as part of a longer moment, one frame in a continuous film of construction and music. NPR singled it out, admiring how the rap carried a confidence unexpected from someone known for other modes. Listeners came to it like neighbors hearing a story through an open window, surprised to find a depth of voice they had not expected and comforted by the restraint of the arrangement. The recording at Capitol Studios, the piano by Christophe Chassol, the repeating synth first heard during the livestream, these facts root the song in a real making, a real room where hands did real work.

Why does it stay with people? Because it is modest and bold at once. It does not shout its truths. It places small truths gently in your lap and trusts you to feel them. The music leaves space for reflection, and the words refuse to tidy themselves into neat moral lessons. For listeners who return, the song becomes a companion for those long slow moments when a memory surfaces and you do not need to explain it, you only need to hold it. It lingers the way a particular light does on a late afternoon, warm and honest and quietly sure that what was just spoken matters.
